entries.914e20d49083278bc6ebc4af57e2e4765769c06b: <div sID="gen18343" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="5" osisID="Lam.5" sID="Lam.5"/> <div eID="gen18343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18344" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18345" type="x-p"/> This chapter, though it has the same number of verses with the 1st, 2nd, and 4th, is not alphabetical, as they were, but the scope of it is the same with that of all the foregoing elegies. We have in it, I. A representation of the present calamitous state of God's people in their captivity, <reference osisRef="Lam.5.1-Lam.5.16">ver. 1-16</reference>. II. A protestation of their concern for God's sanctuary, as that which lay nearer their heart than any secular interest of their own, <reference osisRef="Lam.5.17-Lam.5.18">ver. 17, 18</reference>. III. A humble supplication to God and expostulation with him, for the returns of mercy (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.19-Lam.5.22">ver. 19-22</reference>); for those that lament and do not pray sin in their lamentations. Some ancient versions call this chapter, "The Prayer of Jeremiah."
entries.30a2d26bff9dba1da6f53aa60ffa6a6ff04b8939: <div eID="gen18345" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18344" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">An Appeal to God; Complicated Sorrows. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 588.)</title> <div sID="gen18346" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Remember, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , what is come upon us: consider, and behold our reproach. <hi type="super">2</hi> Our inheritance is turned to strangers, our houses to aliens. <hi type="super">3</hi> We are orphans and fatherless, our mothers <hi type="italic">are</hi> as widows. <hi type="super">4</hi> We have drunken our water for money; our wood is sold unto us. <hi type="super">5</hi> Our necks <hi type="italic">are</hi> under persecution: we labour, <hi type="italic">and</hi> have no rest. <hi type="super">6</hi> We have given the hand <hi type="italic">to</hi> the Egyptians, <hi type="italic">and to</hi> the Assyrians, to be satisfied with bread. <hi type="super">7</hi> Our fathers have sinned, <hi type="italic">and are</hi> not; and we have borne their iniquities. <hi type="super">8</hi> Servants have ruled over us: <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none that doth deliver <hi type="italic">us</hi> out of their hand. <hi type="super">9</hi> We gat our bread with <hi type="italic">the peril of</hi> our lives because of the sword of the wilderness. <hi type="super">10</hi> Our skin was black like an oven because of the terrible famine. <hi type="super">11</hi> They ravished the women in Zion, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the maids in the cities of Judah. <hi type="super">12</hi> Princes are hanged up by their hand: the faces of elders were not honoured. <hi type="super">13</hi> They took the young men to grind, and the children fell under the wood. <hi type="super">14</hi> The elders have ceased from the gate, the young men from their music. <hi type="super">15</hi> The joy of our heart is ceased; our dance is turned into mourning. <hi type="super">16</hi> The crown is fallen <hi type="italic">from</hi> our head: woe unto us, that we have sinned! <div eID="gen18346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18347" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Is any afflicted? let him pray;</hi> and let him in prayer pour out his complaint to God, and make known before him his trouble. The people of God do so here; being overwhelmed with grief, they give vent to their sorrows at the footstool of the throne of grace, and so give themselves ease. They complain not of evils feared, but of evils felt: "<hi type="italic">Remember what has come upon us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.5.1">v. 1</reference>. What was of old threatened against us, and was long in the coming, has now at length <hi type="italic">come upon us,</hi> and we are ready to sink under it. <hi type="italic">Remember what is</hi> past, <hi type="italic">consider and behold</hi> what is present, and <hi type="italic">let not all the trouble</hi> we are in <hi type="italic">seem little to thee,</hi> and not worth taking notice of," <reference osisRef="Neh.9.32">Neh. ix. 32</reference>. Note, As it is a great comfort to us, so it ought to be a sufficient one, in our troubles, that God sees, and considers, and remembers, all that <hi type="italic">has come upon us;</hi> and in our prayers we need only to recommend our case to his gracious and compassionate consideration. The one word in which all their grievances are summer up is <hi type="italic">reproach: Consider, and behold our reproach.</hi> The troubles they were in compared with their former dignity and plenty, were a greater reproach to them than they would have been to any other people, especially considering their relation to God and dependence upon him, and his former appearances for them; and therefore this they complain of very sensibly, because, as it was a reproach, it reflected upon the name and honour of that God who had owned them for his people. <hi type="italic">And what wilt thou do unto thy great name?</hi> <div eID="gen18347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18348" type="x-p"/> I. They acknowledge the reproach of sin which they bear, <hi type="italic">the reproach of their youth</hi> (which Ephraim bemoans himself for, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.19">Jer. xxxi. 19</reference>), of the early days of their nation. This comes in in the midst of their complaints (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.7">v. 7</reference>), but may well be put in the front of them: <hi type="italic">Our fathers have sinned and are not;</hi> they are dead and gone, but <hi type="italic">we have borne their iniquities.</hi> This is not here a peevish complaint, nor an imputation of unrighteousness to God, like that which we have, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.29">Jer. xxxi. 29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.2">Ezek. xviii. 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">The fathers did eat sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge,</hi> and therefore <hi type="italic">the ways of the Lord are not equal.</hi> But it is a penitent confession of the sins of their ancestors, which they themselves also had persisted in, for which they now justly suffered; the judgments God brought upon them were so very great that it appeared that God had in them an eye to the sins of their ancestors (because they had not been remarkably punished in this world) as well as to their own sins; and thus God was justified both in his connivance at their ancestors (he <hi type="italic">laid up their iniquity for their children</hi>) and in his severity with them, on whom he visited that iniquity, <reference osisRef="Matt.23.35-Matt.23.36">Matt. xxiii. 35, 36</reference>. Thus they do here, 1. Submit themselves to the divine justice: "Lord, thou art just in all that is brought upon us, for we are a seed of evil doers, children of wrath, and heirs of the curse; we are sinful, and we have it by kind." Note, The sins which God looks back upon in punishing we must look back upon in repenting, and must take notice of all that which will help to justify God in correcting us. 2. They refer themselves to the divine pity: "Lord, <hi type="italic">our fathers have sinned,</hi> and we justly smart for their sins; but <hi type="italic">they are not;</hi> they were taken away from the evil to come; they lived not to see and share in these miseries that have <hi type="italic">come upon us,</hi> and we are left to <hi type="italic">bear their iniquities.</hi> Now, though herein God is righteous, yet it must be owned that our case is pitiable, and worthy of compassion." Note, If we be penitent and patient under what we suffer for the sins of our fathers, we may expect that he who punishes will pity, and will soon return in mercy to us. <div eID="gen18348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18349" type="x-p"/> II. They represent the reproach of trouble which they bear, in divers particulars, which tend much to their disgrace. <div eID="gen18349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18350" type="x-p"/> 1. They are disseised of that good land which God gave them, and their enemies have got possession of it, <reference osisRef="Lam.5.2">v. 2</reference>. Canaan was their inheritance; it was theirs by promise. God gave it to them and their seed, and they held it by grant from his crown, (<reference osisRef="Ps.136.21-Ps.136.22">Ps. cxxxvi. 21, 22</reference>); but now, "It is turned to strangers; those possess it who have no right to it, who are <hi type="italic">strangers to the commonwealth of Israel and aliens from the covenants of promise;</hi> they dwell in the houses that we built, and this is our reproach." It is the happiness of all God's spiritual Israel that the heavenly Canaan is an inheritance that they cannot be disseised of, that shall never be turned to strangers. <div eID="gen18350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18351" type="x-p"/> 2. Their state and nation are brought into a condition like that of widows and orphans (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.3">v. 3</reference>): "<hi type="italic">We are fatherless</hi> (that is, helpless); we have none to protect us, to provide for us, to take any care of us. Our king, who is the father of the country, is cut off; nay, God our Father seems to have forsaken us and cast us off; <hi type="italic">our mothers,</hi> our cities, that were as fruitful mothers in Israel, <hi type="italic">are</hi> now <hi type="italic">as widows,</hi> are as wives whose husbands are dead, destitute of comfort, and exposed to wrong and injury, and this is our reproach; for we who made a figure are now looked on with contempt." <div eID="gen18351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18352" type="x-p"/> 3. They are put hard to it to provide necessaries for themselves and their families, whereas once they lived in abundance and had plenty of every thing. Water used to be free and easily come by, but now (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.4">v. 4</reference>), <hi type="italic">We have drunk our water for money,</hi> and the saying is no longer true, <hi type="italic">Usus communis aquarum</hi>—<hi type="italic">Water is free to all.</hi> So hardly did their oppressors use them that they could not have a draught of fair water but they must purchase it either with money or with work. Formerly they had fuel too for the fetching; but now, "<hi type="italic">Our wood is sold to us,</hi> and we pay dearly for every faggot." Now were they punished for employing their children to gather wood for fire with which to <hi type="italic">bake cakes for the queen of heaven,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.7.18">Jer. vii. 18</reference>. They were perfectly proscribed by their oppressors, were forbidden the use both of fire and water, according to the ancient form, <hi type="italic">Interdico tibi aqua et igni</hi>—<hi type="italic">I forbid thee the use of water and fire.</hi> But what must they do for bread? Truly that was as hard to come at as any thing, for (1.) Some of them sold their liberty for it (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.6">v. 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">We have given the hand to the Egyptians and to the Assyrians,</hi> have made the best bargain we could with them, to serve them, that we might <hi type="italic">be satisfied with bread.</hi> We were glad to submit to the meanest employment, upon the hardest terms, to get a sorry livelihood; we have yielded ourselves to be their vassals, have parted with all to them, as the Egyptians did to Pharaoh in the years of famine, that we might have something for ourselves and families to subsist on." The neighbouring nations used to trade with Judah for wheat (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.17">Ezek. xxvii. 17</reference>), for it was a fruitful land; but now it <hi type="italic">eats up the inhabitants,</hi> and they are glad to make court to the Egyptians and Assyrians. (2.) Others of them ventured their lives for it (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">We got our bread with the peril of our lives;</hi> when, being straitened by the siege and all provisions cut off, they either sallied or stole out of the city, to fetch in some supply, they were in danger of falling into the hands of the besiegers and being put to the sword, <hi type="italic">the sword of the wilderness</hi> it is called, or <hi type="italic">of the plain</hi> (for so the word signifies), the besiegers lying dispersed every where in the plains that were about the city. Let us take occasion hence to bless God for the plenty that we enjoy, that we get our bread so easily, scarcely with the sweat of our face, much less <hi type="italic">with the peril of our lives;</hi> and for the peace we enjoy, that we can go out, and enjoy not only the necessary productions, but the pleasures of the country, without any fear of <hi type="italic">the sword of the wilderness.</hi> <div eID="gen18352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18353" type="x-p"/> 4. Those are brought into slavery who were a free people, and not only their own masters, but masters of all about them, and this is as much as any thing their reproach (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">Our necks are under</hi> the grievous and intolerable yoke of <hi type="italic">persecution</hi> (the iron yoke which Jeremiah foretold should be laid upon them, <reference osisRef="Jer.28.14">Jer. xxviii. 14</reference>); we are used like beasts in the yoke, that wholly serve their owners, and are at the command of their drivers. That which aggravated the servitude was, (1.) That their labours were incessant, like those of Israel in Egypt, who were daily tasked, nay, overtasked: <hi type="italic">We labour and have no rest,</hi> neither leave nor leisure to rest. The oxen in the yoke are unyoked at night and have rest; so they have, by a particular provision of the law, on the sabbath day; but the poor captives in Babylon, who were compelled to work for their living, <hi type="italic">laboured and had no rest,</hi> no night's rest, no sabbath-rest; they were quite tired out with continual toil. (2.) That their masters were insufferable (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Servants have ruled over us;</hi> and nothing is more vexatious than <hi type="italic">a servant when he reigns,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.30.22">Prov. xxx. 22</reference>. They were not only the great men of the Chaldeans that commanded them, but even the meanest of their servants abused them at pleasure, and insulted over them; and they must be at their beck too. The curse of Canaan had now become the doom of Judah: <hi type="italic">A servant of servants shall he be.</hi> They would not be ruled by their God, and by his servants the prophets, whose rule was gentle and gracious, and therefore justly are they ruled with rigour by their enemies and their servants. (3.) That they saw no probable way for the redress of their grievances: "<hi type="italic">There is none that doth deliver us out of their hand;</hi> not only none to rescue us out of our captivity, but none to check and restrain the insolence of the servants that abuse us and trample upon us," which one would think their masters should have done, because it was a usurpation of their authority; but, it should seem, they connived at it and encouraged it, and, as if they were not worthy of the correction of gentlemen, they are turned over to the footmen to be spurned by them. Well might they pray, <hi type="italic">Lord, consider and behold our reproach.</hi> <div eID="gen18353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18354" type="x-p"/> 5. Those who used to be feasted are now famished (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">Our skin was black like an oven,</hi> dried and parched too, <hi type="italic">because of the terrible famine,</hi> the <hi type="italic">storms of famine</hi> (so the word is); for, though famine comes gradually upon a people, yet it comes violently, and bears down all before it, and there is no resisting it; and this also is their disgrace; hence we read of <hi type="italic">the reproach of famine,</hi> which in captivity their received among the heathen, <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.30">Ezek. xxxvi. 30</reference>. <div eID="gen18354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18355" type="x-p"/> 6. All sorts of people, even those whose persons and characters were most inviolable, were abused and dishonoured. (1.) The <hi type="italic">women</hi> were <hi type="italic">ravished,</hi> even <hi type="italic">the women in Zion,</hi> that holy mountain, <reference osisRef="Lam.5.11">v. 11</reference>. The committing of such abominable wickednesses there is very justly and sadly complained of. (2.) The great men were not only put to death, but put to ignominious deaths. <hi type="italic">Princes were hanged,</hi> as if they had been slaves, <hi type="italic">by the hands</hi> of the Chaldeans (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.12">v. 12</reference>), who took a pride in doing this barbarous execution with <hi type="italic">their own hands.</hi> Some think that the dead bodies of the princes, after they were slain with the sword, were hung up, as the bodies of Saul's sons, in disgrace to them, and as it were to expiate the nation's guilt. (3.) No respect was shown to magistrates and those in authority: <hi type="italic">The faces of elders,</hi> elders in age, elders in office, <hi type="italic">were not honoured.</hi> This will be particularly remembered against the Chaldeans another day. <reference osisRef="Isa.47.6">Isa. xlvii. 6</reference>, <hi type="italic">Upon the ancient hast thou very heavily laid thy yoke.</hi> (4.) The tenderness of youth was no more considered than the gravity of old age (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">They took the young men to grind</hi> at the hand-mills, nay, perhaps at the horse-mills. <hi type="italic">The young men have carried the grist</hi> (so some), <hi type="italic">have carried the mill,</hi> or <hi type="italic">mill-stones,</hi> so others. They loaded them as if they had been beasts of burden, and so broke their backs while they were young, and made the rest of their lives the more miserable. Nay, they made <hi type="italic">the</hi> little <hi type="italic">children</hi> carry their wood home for fuel, and laid such burdens upon them that they <hi type="italic">fell</hi> down <hi type="italic">under</hi> them, so very inhuman were these cruel taskmasters! <div eID="gen18355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18356" type="x-p"/> 7. An end was put to all their gladness, and their joy was quite extinguished (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">The young men,</hi> who used to be disposed to mirth, have ceased <hi type="italic">from their music,</hi> have hung their harps upon the willow-trees. It does indeed well become old men to cease from their music; it is time to lay it by with a gracious contempt when <hi type="italic">all the daughters of music are brought low;</hi> but it speaks some great calamity upon a people when their young men are made to cease from it. It was so with the body of the people (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">The joy of their heart ceased;</hi> they never knew what joy was since the enemy came in upon them like a flood, for ever since <hi type="italic">deep called unto deep,</hi> and one wave flowed in upon the neck of another, so that they were quite overwhelmed: <hi type="italic">Our dance is turned into mourning,</hi> instead of leaping for joy, as formerly, we sink and lie down in sorrow. This may refer especially to the joy of their solemn feasts, and the dancing used in them (<reference osisRef="Judg.21.21">Judg. xxi. 21</reference>), which was not only modest, but sacred, dancing; this was <hi type="italic">turned into mourning,</hi> which was doubled on their festival days, in remembrance of their former pleasant things. <div eID="gen18356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18357" type="x-p"/> 8. An end was put to all their glory. (1.) The public administration of justice was their glory, but that was gone: <hi type="italic">The elders have ceased from the gate</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.14">v. 14</reference>); the course of justice, which used to run down like a river, is now stopped; the courts of justice, which used to be kept with so much solemnity, are put down; for the judges are slain, or carried captive. (2.) The royal dignity was their glory, but that also was gone: <hi type="italic">The crown has fallen from our head,</hi> not only the <hi type="italic">king</hi> himself fallen into disgrace, but <hi type="italic">the crown;</hi> he has no successor; the regalia are all lost. Note, Earthly crowns are fading falling things; but, blessed be God, there is <hi type="italic">a crown of glory that fades not away,</hi> that never falls, <hi type="italic">a kingdom that cannot be moved.</hi> Upon this complaint, but with reference to all the foregoing complaints, they make that penitent acknowledgment, "<hi type="italic">Woe unto us that we have sinned!</hi> Alas for us! Our case is very deplorable, and it is all owing to ourselves; we are undone, and, which aggravates the matter, we are undone by our own hands. God is righteous, for <hi type="italic">we have sinned.</hi>" Note, All our woes are owing to our own sin and folly. If <hi type="italic">the crown of our head be fallen</hi> (for so the words run), if we lose our excellency and become mean, we may thank ourselves, we have by our own iniquity profaned our crown and <hi type="italic">laid our honour in the dust.</hi>
entries.39d485dc2998f272b25b9d5137a2a3fdd4bad641: <div eID="gen18357" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Unchangeableness of God; Prayer for Mercy and Grace. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 588.)</title> <div sID="gen18358" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> For this our heart is faint; for these <hi type="italic">things</hi> our eyes are dim. <hi type="super">18</hi> Because of the mountain of Zion, which is desolate, the foxes walk upon it. <hi type="super">19</hi> Thou, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , remainest for ever; thy throne from generation to generation. <hi type="super">20</hi> Wherefore dost thou forget us for ever, <hi type="italic">and</hi> forsake us so long time? <hi type="super">21</hi> Turn thou us unto thee, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , and we shall be turned; renew our days as of old. <hi type="super">22</hi> But thou hast utterly rejected us; thou art very wroth against us. <div eID="gen18358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18359" type="x-p"/> Here, I. The people of God express the deep concern they had for the ruins of the temple, more than for any other of their calamities; the interests of God's house lay nearer their hearts than those of their own (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.17-Lam.5.18">v. 17, 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">For this our heart is faint,</hi> and sinks under the load of its own heaviness; <hi type="italic">for these things our eyes are dim,</hi> and our sight is gone, as is usual in a deliquium, or fainting fit. "It is <hi type="italic">because of the mountain of Zion, which is desolate,</hi> the holy mountain, and the temple built upon that mountain. For other desolations our hearts grieve and our eyes weep; but for this our hearts faint and our eyes are dim." Note, Nothing lies so heavily upon the spirits of good people as that which threatens the ruin of religion or weakens its interests; and it is a comfort if we can appeal to God that that afflicts us more than any temporal affliction to ourselves. "The people have polluted the <hi type="italic">mountain of Zion</hi> with their sins, and therefore God has justly made it <hi type="italic">desolate,</hi> to such a degree that <hi type="italic">the foxes walk upon it</hi> as freely and commonly as they do in the woods." It is sad indeed when the <hi type="italic">mountain of Zion</hi> has become <hi type="italic">a portion for foxes</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.63.10">Ps. lxiii. 10</reference>); but sin had first made it so, <reference osisRef="Ezek.13.4">Ezek. xiii. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen18359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18360" type="x-p"/> II. They comfort themselves with the doctrine of God's eternity, and the perpetuity of his government (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.19">v. 19</reference>): But <hi type="italic">thou, O Lord! remainest for ever.</hi> This they are taught to do by that psalm which is entitled, <hi type="italic">A prayer of the afflicted,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.102.27-Ps.102.28">Ps. cii. 27, 28</reference>. When all our creature-comforts are removed from us, and our hearts fail us, we may then encourage ourselves with the belief, 1. Of God's eternity: <hi type="italic">Thou remainest for ever.</hi> What shakes the world gives no disturbance to him who made it; whatever revolutions there are on earth there is no change in the Eternal Mind; God is still the same, and <hi type="italic">remains for ever</hi> infinitely wise and holy, just and good; with him there is <hi type="italic">no variableness nor shadow of turning.</hi> 2. Of the never-failing continuance of his dominion: <hi type="italic">Thy throne is from generation to generation;</hi> the throne of glory, the throne of grace, and the throne of government, are all unchangeable, immovable; and this is matter of comfort to us when <hi type="italic">the crown has fallen from our head.</hi> When the thrones of princes, that should be our protectors, are brought to the dust, and buried in it, God's throne continues still; he still rules the world, and rules it for the good of the church. The Lord reigns, reigns for ever, even <hi type="italic">thy God, O Zion!</hi> <div eID="gen18360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18361" type="x-p"/> III. They humbly expostulate with God concerning the low condition they were now in, and the frowns of heaven they were now under (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.20">v. 20</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Wherefore dost thou forsake us so long time,</hi> as if we were quite deprived of the tokens of thy presence? Wherefore dost thou defer our deliverance, as if thou hadst utterly abandoned us? Thou art the same, and, though the throne of thy sanctuary is demolished, thy throne in heaven is unshaken. But wilt thou not be the same to us?" Not as if they thought God had forgotten and forsaken them, much less feared his forgetting and forsaking them for ever; but thus they express the value they had for his favour and presence, which they thought it long that they were deprived of the evidence and comfort of. The <reference osisRef="Lam.5.22">last verse</reference> may be read as such an expostulation, and so the margin reads it: "<hi type="italic">For wilt thou utterly reject us? Wilt thou be perpetually wroth with us,</hi> not only not smile upon us and remember us in mercy, but frown upon us and lay us under the tokens of thy wrath, not only not draw nigh to us, but cast us out of thy presence and forbid us to draw nigh unto thee? How ill this be reconciled with thy goodness and faithfulness, and the stability of thy covenant?" We read it, "<hi type="italic">But thou hast rejected us;</hi> thou hast given us cause to fear that thou hast. Lord, how long shall we be in this temptation?" Note, Thou we may not quarrel with God, yet we may plead with him; and, though we may not conclude that he has cast off, yet we may (with the prophet, <reference osisRef="Jer.12.1">Jer. xii. 1</reference>) humbly reason with him concerning his judgments, especially the continuance of the desolations of his sanctuary. <div eID="gen18361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18362" type="x-p"/> IV. They earnestly pray to God for mercy and grace: "Lord, do not reject <hi type="italic">us for ever,</hi> but <hi type="italic">turn thou us unto thee; renew our days,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Lam.5.21">v. 21</reference>. Though these words are not put last, yet the Rabbin, because they would not have the book to conclude with those melancholy words (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.22">v. 22</reference>), repeat this prayer again, that the sun may not set under a cloud, and so make these the last words both in writing and reading this chapter. They here pray, 1. For converting grace to prepare and qualify them for mercy: <hi type="italic">Turn us to thee, O Lord!</hi> They had complained that God had forsaken and forgotten them, and then their prayer is not, <hi type="italic">Turn thou to us,</hi> but, <hi type="italic">Turn us to thee,</hi> which implies an acknowledgment that the cause of the distance was in themselves. God never leaves any till they first leave him, nor stands afar off from any longer than while they stand afar off from him; if therefore he turn them to him in a way of duty, no doubt but he will quickly return to them in a way of mercy. This agrees with that repeated prayer (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.3">Ps. lxxx. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.80.7">7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.80.19">19</reference>), <hi type="italic">Turn us again, and then cause thy face to shine. Turn us</hi> from our idols to thyself, by a sincere repentance and reformation, <hi type="italic">and</hi> then <hi type="italic">we shall be turned.</hi> This implies a further acknowledgment of their own weakness and inability to turn themselves. There is in our nature a proneness to backslide from God, but no disposition to return to him till his grace works in us both <hi type="italic">to will and to do.</hi> So necessary is that grace that we may truly say, <hi type="italic">Turn us or we shall not be turned,</hi> but shall wander endlessly; and so powerful and effectual is that grace that we may as truly say, <hi type="italic">Turn us, and we shall be turned;</hi> for it is a day of power, almighty power, in which God's people are made a <hi type="italic">willing people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.110.3">Ps. cx. 3</reference>. 2. For restoring mercy: <hi type="italic">Turn us to thee,</hi> and then <hi type="italic">renew our days as of old,</hi> put us into the same happy state that our ancestors were in long ago and that they continued long in; let it be with us as it was <hi type="italic">at the first,</hi> and <hi type="italic">at the beginning,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.1.26">Isa. i. 26</reference>. Note, If God by his grace renew our hearts, he will be his favour <hi type="italic">renew our days,</hi> so that we shall <hi type="italic">renew our youth as the eagle,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.103.5">Ps. ciii. 5</reference>. Those that <hi type="italic">repent, and do their first works,</hi> shall rejoice, and recover their first comforts. God's mercies to his people have been <hi type="italic">ever of old</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.6">Ps. xxv. 6</reference>); and therefore they may hope, even then when he seems to have forsaken and forgotten them, that the mercy which was <hi type="italic">from everlasting</hi> will be <hi type="italic">to everlasting.</hi>  <chapter eID="Lam.5"/> <div eID="gen18362" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen18236" osisID="Lam" type="book"/>

entries.8e4a2d49ca82b33f34a99fcdb2b4001274172d97: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10921"/><title type="x-s">CHAPTER (ELEGY) 5</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Lam.5.1-Lam.5.22">La 5:1-22</reference>. Epiphonema, or a Closing Recapitulation of the Calamities Treated in the Previous Elegies.</title> <div sID="gen19670" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10921"/>1. (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.50">Psa 89:50</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.51">51</reference>). <div eID="gen19670" type="x-p"/>
entries.54c57ab57287a54136f7ffc407e24b9c58c25acd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10922"/><div sID="gen19671" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10922"/><hi type="bold">2. Our inheritance--</hi>"Thine inheritance" (<reference osisRef="Ps.79.1">Psa 79:1</reference>). The land given of old to us by Thy gift. <div eID="gen19671" type="x-p"/>
entries.2addb23819a021f31b934f69b13efcf03eb84882: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10923"/><div sID="gen19672" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10923"/><hi type="bold">3. fatherless--</hi>Our whole land is full of orphans [Calvin]. Or, "we are fatherless," being abandoned by Thee our "Father" (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.19">Jr 3:19</reference>), [Grotius]. <div eID="gen19672" type="x-p"/>
entries.a4b224347d397e19be3ffa502616e4b957225694: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10924"/><div sID="gen19673" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10924"/><hi type="bold">4. water for money--</hi>The Jews were compelled to pay the enemy for the water of their own cisterns after the overthrow of Jerusalem; or rather, it refers to their sojourn in Babylon; they had to pay tax for access to the rivers and fountains. Thus, "our" means the water which we need, the commonest necessary of life.<div eID="gen19673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19674" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">our wood--</hi>In Judea each one could get wood without pay; in Babylon, "our wood," the wood we need, must be paid for. <div eID="gen19674" type="x-p"/>
entries.6eb875812a81122d756db18d5ec4353179216502: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10925"/><div sID="gen19675" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10925"/>5. Literally, "On our necks we are persecuted"; that is, Men tread on our necks (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.12">Psa 66:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.51.23">Is 51:23</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Josh.10.24">Jos 10:24</reference>). The extremest oppression. The foe not merely galled the Jews face, back, and sides, but their neck. A just retribution, as they had been stiff in neck against the yoke of God (<reference osisRef="2Chr.30.8">2Ch 30:8</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Neh.9.29">Ne 9:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.48.4">Is 48:4</reference>). <div eID="gen19675" type="x-p"/>
entries.19a1393ab49fa2e5fcad232cb0953d452f4f7cc8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10926"/><div sID="gen19676" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10926"/><hi type="bold">6. given ... hand to--</hi>in token of submission (see on <reference osisRef="Jer.50.15">Jr 50:15</reference>).<div eID="gen19676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19677" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to ... Egyptians--</hi>at the death of Josiah (<reference osisRef="2Chr.36.3">2Ch 36:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.4">4</reference>).<div eID="gen19677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19678" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Assyrians--</hi>that is, the Chaldeans who occupied the empire which Assyria had held. So <reference osisRef="Jer.2.18">Jr 2:18</reference>.<div eID="gen19678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19679" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to be satisfied with bread--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.28.48">De 28:48</reference>). <div eID="gen19679" type="x-p"/>
entries.952abd00b4909bad1131a5e60b6479983100b7df: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10927"/><div sID="gen19680" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10927"/>7. (<reference osisRef="Jer.31.29">Jr 31:29</reference>).<div eID="gen19680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19681" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">borne their iniquities--</hi>that is, the punishment of them. The accumulated sins of our fathers from age to age, as well as our own, are visited on us. They say this as a plea why God should pity them (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.2">Eze 18:2</reference>, &c.). <div eID="gen19681" type="x-p"/>
entries.c90f5efac13a89772acf1137de6fdf4f05a6462b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10928"/><div sID="gen19682" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10928"/><hi type="bold">8. Servants ... ruled ... us--</hi>Servants under the Chaldean governors ruled the Jews (<reference osisRef="Neh.5.15">Ne 5:15</reference>). Israel, once a "kingdom of priests" (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.6">Ex 19:6</reference>), is become like Canaan, "a servant of servants," according to the curse (<reference osisRef="Gen.9.25">Ge 9:25</reference>). The Chaldeans were designed to be "servants" of Shem, being descended from Ham (<reference osisRef="Gen.9.26">Ge 9:26</reference>). Now through the Jews' sin, their positions are reversed. <div eID="gen19682" type="x-p"/>
entries.09472bc172cb87c636bc05befe9b30e08dc0d880: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10929"/><div sID="gen19683" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10929"/><hi type="bold">9. We gat our bread with ... peril--</hi>that is, those of us left in the city after its capture by the Chaldeans.<div eID="gen19683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19684" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because of ... sword of ... wilderness--</hi>because of the liability to attack by the robber Arabs of the wilderness, through which the Jews had to pass to get "bread" from Egypt (compare <reference osisRef="Lam.5.6">La 5:6</reference>). <div eID="gen19684" type="x-p"/>
entries.10ce2e256e481f7df95e06e769a011eac01864fe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10930"/><div sID="gen19685" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10930"/>10. As an oven is scorched with too much fire, so our skin with the hot blast of famine (Margin, rightly, "storms," like the hot simoom). Hunger dries up the pores so that the skin becomes like as if it were scorched by the sun (<reference osisRef="Job.30.30">Job 30:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.119.83">Psa 119:83</reference>). <div eID="gen19685" type="x-p"/>
entries.e7913c0283f2fcd14721fe8d46e189de60260340: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10931"/><div sID="gen19686" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10931"/>11. So in just retribution Babylon itself should fare in the end. Jerusalem shall for the last time suffer these woes before her final restoration (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.2">Zec 14:2</reference>). <div eID="gen19686" type="x-p"/>
entries.81583bd49748dfa68988160cf268c485450e4477: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10932"/><div sID="gen19687" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10932"/><hi type="bold">12. hanged ... by their hand--</hi>a piece of wanton cruelty invented by the Chaldeans. Grotius translates, "Princes were hung by the hand of the enemy"; hanging was a usual mode of execution (<reference osisRef="Gen.40.19">Ge 40:19</reference>).<div eID="gen19687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19688" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">elders--</hi>officials (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.16">La 4:16</reference>). <div eID="gen19688" type="x-p"/>
entries.eeddedf91104dd8e262357c06271b1ed09b70f26: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10933"/><div sID="gen19689" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10933"/><hi type="bold">13. young men ... grind--</hi>The work of the lowest female slave was laid on young men (<reference osisRef="Judg.16.21">Jud 16:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.31.10">Job 31:10</reference>).<div eID="gen19689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19690" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">children fell under ... wood--</hi>Mere children had to bear burdens of wood so heavy that they sank beneath them. <div eID="gen19690" type="x-p"/>
entries.bd9e8770f0a30e35a1453a24a575b2d9246340b2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10934"/><div sID="gen19691" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10934"/>14. Aged men in the East meet in the open space round the gate to decide judicial trials and to hold social converse (<reference osisRef="Job.29.7">Job 29:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.29.8">8</reference>). <div eID="gen19691" type="x-p"/>
entries.f9b930113dbbf9ddbbf9e670bf8c411f0cd5c1bc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10935"/><div sID="gen19692" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10935"/><hi type="bold">16. The crown--</hi>all our glory, the kingdom and the priesthood (<reference osisRef="Job.19.9">Job 19:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.89.39">Psa 89:39</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.44">44</reference>). <div eID="gen19692" type="x-p"/>
entries.568dc60f92bbda371336be569c808cce90692261: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10936"/><div sID="gen19693" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10936"/>17. (<reference osisRef="Lam.1.22">La 1:22</reference>; 2:11). <div eID="gen19693" type="x-p"/>
entries.413361037724984d27631746eff077bd7f86b554: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10937"/><div sID="gen19694" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10937"/><hi type="bold">18. foxes--</hi>They frequent desolate places where they can freely and fearlessly roam. <div eID="gen19694" type="x-p"/>
entries.3f60dd0613a85b1e3367a6a6811da495210f3f97: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10938"/><div sID="gen19695" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10938"/>19. (<reference osisRef="Ps.102.12">Psa 102:12</reference>). The perpetuity of God's rule over human affairs, however He may seem to let His people be oppressed for a time, is their ground of hope of restoration. <div eID="gen19695" type="x-p"/>
entries.cb2bf5e20ffe91c77742f26d1d27cf437a0bfd08: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10939"/><div sID="gen19696" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10939"/><hi type="bold">20. for ever--</hi>that is, for "so long a time." <div eID="gen19696" type="x-p"/>
entries.9ce6f6208c6e818d39a1d29f93cab77c76dba0c6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10940"/><div sID="gen19697" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10940"/>21. (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.3">Psa 80:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.31.18">Jr 31:18</reference>). "Restore us to favor with Thee, and so we shall be restored to our old position" [Grotius]. Jeremiah is not speaking of spiritual conversion, but of that outward turning whereby God receives men into His fatherly favor, manifested in bestowing prosperity [Calvin]. Still, as Israel is a type of the Church, temporal goods typify spiritual blessings; and so the sinner may use this prayer for God to convert him. <div eID="gen19697" type="x-p"/>
entries.15cdb5114c076ed70d8af059ab893e9b4b705135: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10941"/><div sID="gen19698" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10941"/><hi type="bold">22. Rather, "Unless haply Thou hast utterly rejected us, and art beyond measure wroth against us," that is, Unless Thou art implacable, which is impossible, hear our prayer [Calvin]. Or, as Margin, "For wouldest Thou utterly reject us?" &c.--</hi>No; that cannot be. The Jews, in this book, and in Isaiah and Malachi, to avoid the ill-omen of a mournful closing sentence, repeat the verse immediately preceding the last [Calvin]. <chapter eID="Lam.5"/><div eID="gen19698" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen19319" osisID="Lam" type="book"/>

entries.238dba670f41fb90519c2a529d9a0055f0b61ddb: <div eID="gen31103" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen31104" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31105" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31105" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31104" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31106" type="x-p"/> This chapter is, as it were, an epiphonema, or conclusion to the four preceding, representing the nation as groaning under their calamities, and humbly supplicating the Divine favor, vv. 1-22. <div eID="gen31106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31107" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen31107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31108" type="x-p"/> Remember, O Lord - In the Vulgate, Syriac, and Arabic, this is headed, "The prayer of Jeremiah." In my old MS. Bible: Here bigynneth the orison of Jeremye the prophete. <div eID="gen31108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31109" type="x-p"/> Though this chapter consists of exactly twenty-two verses, the number of letters in the Hebrew alphabet, yet the acrostic form is no longer observed. Perhaps any thing so technical was not thought proper when in agony and distress (under a sense of God's displeasure on account of sin) they prostrated themselves before him to ask for mercy. Be this as it may, no attempt appears to have been made to throw these verses into the form of the preceding chapters. It is properly a solemn prayer of all the people, stating their past and present sufferings, and praying for God's mercy. <div eID="gen31109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31110" type="x-p"/> Behold our reproach - הביט hebita. But many MSS. of Kennicott's, and the oldest of my own, add the ה he paragogic, הביטה hebitah, "Look down earnestly with commiseration;" for paragogic letters always increase the sense.
entries.52784a6f6ffd223e45b6c4b2a38f384c0aa327ad: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen31110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31111" type="x-p"/> Our inheritance is turned to strangers - The greater part of the Jews were either slain or carried away captive; and even those who were left under Gedaliah were not free, for they were vassals to the Chaldeans.
entries.be18862add9042d39858076042bc70bd64d459f0: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen31111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31112" type="x-p"/> We have drunken our water for money - I suppose the meaning of this is, that every thing was taxed by the Chaldeans, and that they kept the management in their own hands, so that wood and water were both sold, the people not being permitted to help themselves. They were now so lowly reduced by servitude, that they were obliged to pay dearly for those things which formerly were common and of no price. A poor Hindoo in the country never buys fire-wood, but when he comes to the city he is obliged to purchase his fuel, and considers it as a matter of great hardship.
entries.a249da1b15122f451ae154ef2939d6b4ae04ad85: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen31112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31113" type="x-p"/> Our necks are under persecution - We feel the yoke of our bondage; we are driven to our work like the bullock, which has a yoke upon his neck.
entries.fb1b6187c8ff7ffefef1f5fd8634ca965ace0f58: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen31113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31114" type="x-p"/> We have given the hand to the Egyptians - We have sought alliances both with the Egyptians and Assyrians, and made covenants with them in order to get the necessaries of life. Or, wherever we are now driven, we are obliged to submit to the people of the countries in order to the preservation of our lives.
entries.159095799fbd19496fe7efc47ba892678f3c149d: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen31114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31115" type="x-p"/> Our fathers have sinned, and are not - Nations, as such, cannot be punished in the other world; therefore national judgments are to be looked for only in this life. The punishment which the Jewish nation had been meriting for a series of years came now upon them, because they copied and increased the sins of their fathers, and the cup of their iniquity was full. Thus the children might be said to bear the sins of the fathers, that is, in temporal punishment, for in no other way does God visit these upon the children. See <reference osisRef="Eze.18.1">Eze 18:1</reference>, etc.
entries.95cadf6875ef0bf19d73f954194c249ee7b202b7: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen31115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31116" type="x-p"/> Servants have ruled over us - To be subject to such is the most painful and dishonorable bondage: - <div eID="gen31116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31117" type="x-p"/> Quio domini faciant, audent cum talia fures? <div eID="gen31117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31118" type="x-p"/> Virg. Ecl. 3:16. "Since slaves so insolent are grown, <div eID="gen31118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31119" type="x-p"/> What may not masters do?" <div eID="gen31119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31120" type="x-p"/> Perhaps he here alludes to the Chaldean soldiers, whose will the wretched Jews were obliged to obey.
entries.649fb522e8cf07bcd4647ffc6d218299e9900508: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen31120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31121" type="x-p"/> We gat our bread with the peril of our lives - They could not go into the wilderness to feed their cattle, or to get the necessaries of life, without being harassed and plundered by marauding parties, and by these were often exposed to the peril of their lives. This was predicted by Moses, <reference osisRef="Deu.28.31">Deu 28:31</reference>.
entries.81f142c9fcb69b3203f0af691a2ecfd2736d27ee: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen31121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31122" type="x-p"/> Our skin was black - because of the terrible famine - Because of the searching winds that burnt up every green thing, destroying vegetation, and in consequence producing a famine.
entries.0a8dad5d223c8159af48b6e4ef20fb43cdd44be8: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen31122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31123" type="x-p"/> They ravished the women in Zion, and the maids in the cities of Judah - The evil mentioned here was predicted by Moses, <reference osisRef="Deu.28.30">Deu 28:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.28.32">Deu 28:32</reference>, and by Jeremiah, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.12">Jer 6:12</reference>.
entries.74453705b7281fe91cc5de1e8f69727a9681732e: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen31123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31124" type="x-p"/> Princes are hanged up by their hand - It is very probable that this was a species of punishment. They were suspended from hooks in the wall by their hands till they died through torture and exhaustion. The body of Saul was fastened to the wall of Bethshan, probably in the same way; but his head had already been taken off. They were hung in this way that they might be devoured by the fowls of the air. It was a custom with the Persians after they had slain, strangled, or beheaded their enemies, to hang their bodies upon poles, or empale them. In this way they treated Histiaeus of Miletum, and Leonidas of Lacedaemon. See Herodot. lib. 6 c. 30, lib. 7 c. 238.
entries.e86e35297b10f554286362abc4647751db3e6cf6: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen31124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31125" type="x-p"/> They took the young men to grind - This was the work of female slaves. See the note on <reference osisRef="Isa.47.2">Isa 47:2</reference>.
entries.4e08ee44096d2dff061be95fa5e37bdca974466a: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen31125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31126" type="x-p"/> The elders have ceased from the gate - There is now no more justice administered to the people; they are under military law, or disposed of in every sense according to the caprice of their masters.
entries.521fb25b44788a22cea694cbe798336af0bc2b52: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen31126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31127" type="x-p"/> The crown is fallen from our head - At feasts, marriages, etc., they used to crown themselves with garlands of flowers; all festivity of this kind was now at an end. Or it may refer to their having lost all sovereignty, being made slaves.
entries.0384ebf7813dd7219d8cd01f15d33fd59d469b85: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen31127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31128" type="x-p"/> The foxes walk upon it - Foxes are very numerous in Palestine, see on <reference osisRef="Jdg.15.4">Jdg 15:4</reference> (note). It was usual among the Hebrews to consider all desolated land to be the resort of wild beasts; which is, in fact, the case every where when the inhabitants are removed from a country.
entries.2275f7f8ca0dba462615b45e13f6cc157f80c37a: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen31128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31129" type="x-p"/> Thou, O Lord, remainest for ever - Thou sufferest no change. Thou didst once love us, O let that love be renewed towards us!
entries.8c295fdffcb32f4a0a4a6e3d4f2898c351028862: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen31129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31130" type="x-p"/> Renew our days as of old - Restore us to our former state. Let us regain our country, our temple, and all the Divine offices of our religion; but, more especially, thy favor.
entries.fe8ac338b61b6aaefc922538621b6cf6439eb40e: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen31130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31131" type="x-p"/> But thou hast utterly rejected us - It appears as if thou hadst sealed our final reprobation, because thou showest against us exceeding great wrath. But convert us, O Lord, onto thee, and we shall be converted. We are now greatly humbled, feel our sin, and see our folly: once more restore us, and we shall never again forsake thee! He heard the prayer; and at the end of seventy years they were restored to their own land. <div eID="gen31131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31132" type="x-p"/> This last verse is well rendered in the first printed edition of our Bible, 1535: - Renue our daies as in olde tyme, for thou hast now banished us longe ynough, and bene sore displeased at us. <div eID="gen31132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31133" type="x-p"/> My old MS. Bible is not less nervous: Newe thou our dais as fro the begynnyng: bot castand aweie thou put us out: thou wrathedist ugein us hugely. <div eID="gen31133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31134" type="x-p"/> Dr. Blayney translates, "For surely thou hast cast us off altogether:" and adds, "כי ki ought certainly to be rendered as causal; God's having rejected his people, and expressed great indignation against them, being the cause and ground of the preceding application, in which they pray to be restored to his favor, and the enjoyment of their ancient privileges." <div eID="gen31134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31135" type="x-p"/> Pareau thinks no good sense can be made of this place unless we translate interrogatively, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.14.19">Jer 14:19</reference> : - "Hast thou utterly rejected Judah? <div eID="gen31135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31136" type="x-p"/> Hath thy soul loathed Sion?" <div eID="gen31136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31137" type="x-p"/> On this ground he translates here, <div eID="gen31137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31138" type="x-p"/> An enim prorsus nos rejecisses? <div eID="gen31138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31139" type="x-p"/> Nobis iratus esses usque adeo? "Hast thou indeed utterly cast us off? <div eID="gen31139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31140" type="x-p"/> Wilt thou be angry with us for ever?" <div eID="gen31140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31141" type="x-p"/> Wilt thou extend thy wrath against us so as to show us no more mercy? This agrees well with the state and feelings of the complainants. <div eID="gen31141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31142" type="x-p"/> Masoretic Notes <div eID="gen31142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31143" type="x-p"/> Number of verses in this Book, 154. <div eID="gen31143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31144" type="x-p"/> Middle verse, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.34">Lam 3:34</reference>. <div eID="gen31144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31145" type="x-p"/> In one of my oldest MSS., the twenty-first verse is repeated at the conclusion of the twenty-second verse. In another, yet older, there is only the first word of it, השיבנו hashibenu, Convert us! <div eID="gen31145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31146" type="x-p"/> Having given in the preceding preface and notes what I judge necessary to explain the principal difficulties in this very fine and affecting poem, very fitly termed The Lamentations, as it justly stands at the head of every composition of the kind, I shall add but a few words, and these shall be by way of recapitulation chiefly. <div eID="gen31146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31147" type="x-p"/> The Hebrews were accustomed to make lamentations or mourning songs upon the death of great men, princes, and heroes, who had distinguished themselves in arms; and upon any occasion or public miseries and calamities. Calmet thinks they had collections of these sorts of Lamentations: and refers in proof to <reference osisRef="2Chr.35.25">2Chr 35:25</reference> : "And Jeremiah lamented for Josiah; and all the singing men and the singing women spake of Josiah in their lamentations, to this day; and made them an ordinance in Israel: and, behold, they are written in the Lamentations." <div eID="gen31147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31148" type="x-p"/> From this verse it is evident, that Jeremiah had composed a funeral elegy on Josiah: but, from the complexion of this Book, it is most evident that it was not composed on the death of Josiah, but upon the desolations of Jerusalem, etc., as has already been noted. His lamentation for Josiah is therefore lost. It appears also, that on particular occasions, perhaps anniversaries, these lamentations were sung by men and women singers, who performed their several parts; for these were all alternate or responsive songs. And it is very likely, that this book was sung in the same way; the men commencing with א aleph, the women responding with ב beth and so on. Several of this sort of songs are still extant. We have those which David composed on the death of his son Absalom, and on the death of his friend Jonathan. And we have those made by Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel, on the desolation of Egypt, Tyre, Sidon, and Babylon. See <reference osisRef="Isa.14.4">Isa 14:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.14.5">Isa 14:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.15.1-Isa.15.9">Isa 15:1-9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.16.1-Isa.16.14">Isa 16:1-14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.7.29">Jer 7:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.9.10">Jer 9:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.48.32">Jer 48:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eze.19.1">Eze 19:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eze.28.11">Eze 28:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eze.32.2">Eze 32:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.9.17">Jer 9:17</reference>. Besides these, we have fragments of others in different places; and references to some, which are now finally lost. <div eID="gen31148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31149" type="x-p"/> In the two first chapters of this book, the prophet describes, principally, the calamities of the siege of Jerusalem. <div eID="gen31149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31150" type="x-p"/> In the third, he deplores the persecutions which he himself had suffered; though he may in this be personifying the city and state; many of his own sufferings being illustrative of the calamities that fell generally upon the city and people at large. <div eID="gen31150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31151" type="x-p"/> The fourth chapter is employed chiefly on the ruin and desolation of the city and temple; and upon the misfortunes of Zedekiah, of whom he speaks in a most respectful, tender, and affecting manner: - "The anointed of Jehovah, the breadth of our nostrils, was taken in their toils, <div eID="gen31151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31152" type="x-p"/> Under whose shadow we said, <div eID="gen31152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31153" type="x-p"/> We shall live among the nations." <div eID="gen31153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31154" type="x-p"/> At the end he speaks of the cruelty of the Edomites, who had insulted Jerusalem in her miseries, and contributed to its demolition. These he threatens with the wrath of God. <div eID="gen31154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31155" type="x-p"/> The fifth chapter is a kind of form of prayer for the Jews, in their dispersions and captivity. In the conclusion of it, he speaks of their fallen royalty; attributes all their calamities to their rebellion and wickedness; and acknowledges that there can be no end to their misery, but in their restoration to the Divine favor. <div eID="gen31155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31156" type="x-p"/> This last chapter was probably written some considerable time after the rest: for it supposes the temple to be so deserted, that the foxes walked undisturbed among its ruins, and that the people were already in captivity. <div eID="gen31156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31157" type="x-p"/> The poem is a monument of the people's iniquity and rebellion; of the displeasure and judgment of God against them; and of the piety, eloquence, and incomparable ability of the poet.  <chapter eID="Lam.5"/> <div eID="gen31157" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen30860" osisID="Lam" type="book"/>

entries.8536cbd2043eda5357910c2f728be01c540d71cb: <reference osisRef="Lam.5.1-Lam.5.7">Lam 5:1-7</reference> <div eID="gen14741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14742" type="x-p"/> Supplication and statement regarding the distress. The quest made in <reference osisRef="Lam.5.1">Lam 5:1</reference> refers to the oppression depicted in what follows. The words, "Remember, O Lord, what hath happened (i.e., befallen) us," are more fully explained in the second member, "Look and behold our disgrace." It is quite arbitrary in Thenius to refer the first member to the past, the second to the present, described in what follows, <reference osisRef="Lam.5.12">Lam 5:12</reference>-16. The <hi type="italic">Qeri</hi> הבּיטה is an unnecessary alteration, after <reference osisRef="Lam.1.11">Lam 1:11</reference>; Lam 3:63. - With <reference osisRef="Lam.5.2">Lam 5:2</reference> begins the description of the disgrace that has befallen them. This consists, first of all, in the fact that their inheritance has become the possession of strangers. Rosenmüller rightly explains נחלה to mean, <hi type="italic">terra quae tuo nobis dono quandam est concessa</hi>. נחפך is used of the transference of the property to others, as in Isa 60:5. Many expositors would refer בּתּינוּ to the houses in Jerusalem which the Chaldeans had not destroyed, on the ground that it is stated, in 2Ki 25:9 and <reference osisRef="Jer.52.13">Jer 52:13</reference>, that the Chaldeans destroyed none but large houses. There is no foundation, however, for this restriction; moreover, it is opposed by the parallel נחלתנוּ. Just as by נחלה we are to understand, not merely the possession of Jerusalem, but of the whole country, so also בּתּינוּ are the dwelling-houses of the country in towns and villages; in this case, the question whether any houses still remained standing in Jerusalem does not demand consideration at all. Nägelsbach is wrong in his remark that נחלה and בּתּים respectively mean immovable and portable property, for houses are certainly not moveable property.
entries.c695ee85880e4f484b760ea42109d8c64da6f3fb: <reference osisRef="Lam.5.8">Lam 5:8</reference> <div eID="gen14745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14746" type="x-p"/> Further description of the miserable condition under which the congregation languishes. Lam 5:8. "Servants rule over us," etc. עבדים are not the Chaldean soldiers, who are in 2Ki 24:10 designated the servants of Nebuchadnezzar (Pareau, Rosenmüller, Maurer); still less the Chaldeans, in so far as they, till shortly before, had been the subjects of the Assyrians (Kalkschmidt); nor the Chaldean satraps, as servants of the king of Babylon (Thenius, Ewald); nor even "slaves who had been employed as overseers and taskmasters of the captives while on the march" (Nägelsbach); but the Chaldeans. These are called servants, partly because of the despotic rule under which they were placed, partly in the sense already indicated by C. B. Michaelis, as being those <hi type="italic">qui nobis potius, si pii fuissemus, servire debuissent</hi>, in accordance with the analogous designation of Jerusalem as a princess among the countries of the world, Lam 1:1.
entries.d1a33be7b99adfba34f7d9ac92e61cc51a87565b: <reference osisRef="Lam.5.9">Lam 5:9</reference> <div eID="gen14746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14747" type="x-p"/> And in addition to this humiliation under dishonourable servitude, we can get our daily bread only at the risk of our life. Thus there is fulfilled to them the threatening in <reference osisRef="Deut.28.28">Deu 28:28</reference>, "Ye shall be servants among your enemies, in hunger and thirst, in nakedness and want of everything." בּנפשׁנוּ, "for the price of our soul," i.e., with our life at stake, we bring in our bread. The danger is more exactly described by what is added: "before the sword of the wilderness." By this expression are meant the predatory Bedouins of the desert, who, falling upon those that were bringing in the bread, plundered, and probably even killed them. The bringing of the bread is not, however, to be referred (with Rosenmüller, Maurer, and Kalkschmidt) to the attempts made to procure bread from the neighbouring countries; still less is it to be referred (with Thenius, Ewald, and Nägelsbach) to the need for "wringing the bread from the desert and its plunderers;" but it refers to the ingathering of the scanty harvest in the country devastated by war and by the visitations of predatory Bedouins: הביא is the word constantly employed in this connection; cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.10">2Sa 9:10</reference>; Hag 1:6.
entries.c89e9425e3f140d67abaf08923ced932c5c05523: <reference osisRef="Lam.5.10">Lam 5:10</reference> <div eID="gen14747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14748" type="x-p"/> The bread which we are thus obliged to struggle for, at the risk of our life, is not even sufficient to allay hunger, which consumes our bodies. נכמר does not mean to be blackened (Chaldee, Kimchi, C. B. Michaelis, Maurer), but in <reference osisRef="Gen.43.30">Gen 43:30</reference>; 1Ki 3:26, and Hos 11:8, to be stirred up (of the bowels, compassion), hence to kindle, glow. This last meaning is required by the comparison with תּנּוּר, oven, furnace. This comparison does not mean <hi type="italic">cutis nostra tanquam fornace adusta est</hi> (Gesenius in <hi type="italic">Thes</hi>., Kalkschmidt), still less "black as an oven" (Dietrich in <hi type="italic">Ges. Lex</hi>.), because תּנּוּר does not mean the oven viewed in respect of its blackness, but (from נוּר) in respect of the fire burning in it. The meaning is, "our skin glows like a baker’s oven" (Vaihinger, Thenius, Nägelsbach, Gerlach), - a strong expression for the fever-heat produced by hunger. As to זלעפות, glowing heat, see on Psa 11:6.
entries.43c2670d3e56149649225b30b50942d0e7debf99: <reference osisRef="Lam.5.11-Lam.5.12">Lam 5:11-12</reference> <div eID="gen14748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14749" type="x-p"/> With this must further be considered the maltreatment which persons of every station, sex, and age have to endure. Lam 5:11. Women and virgins are dishonoured in Jerusalem, and in the other cities of the land. Lam 5:12. Princes are suspended by the hand of the enemy (Ewald, contrary to the use of language, renders "along with" them). To hang those who had been put to death was something superadded to the simple punishment by death (Deu 21:22.), and so far as a shameful kind of execution. "The old men are not honoured," i.e., dishonoured; cf. <reference osisRef="Lam.4.16">Lam 4:16</reference>; Lev 19:32. The words are not to be restricted to the events mentioned in <reference osisRef="Jer.39.6">Jer 39:6</reference>, but also apply to the present condition of those who are complaining,
entries.4cc13df0dbeb8afb2e926aa23428ebca3d1eb49f: <reference osisRef="Lam.5.13-Lam.5.14">Lam 5:13-14</reference> <div eID="gen14749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14750" type="x-p"/> Youths and boys are forced to engage in heavy servile work. טחון נשׂאוּ does not mean "they take them for the mill," <hi type="italic">ad molendum sumpserunt</hi> (Ewald, Rosenmüller). Apart from the consideration that there is no ground for it in the language employed, such a view of the words does not accord with the parallelism. נשׂא, construed with a simple infinitive or accusative (without ל), does not mean "to take for something." טחון is a substantive, "the mill." "To bear (carry) the mill" signifies to work at and with the mill. We must think of the hand-mill, which was found in every household, and which could thus be carried from one place to another. Grinding was the work of salves; see on Jdg 16:21. The carrying of the mill (not merely of the upper millstone) is mentioned as the heaviest portion of the work in grinding. "Boys stagger (fall down) on the wood laid on them to be carried," i.e., under the burden of it. כּשׁל with בּ means to stumble on something; here בּ denotes the cause of the stumbling; cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.6.21">Jer 6:21</reference>; Lev 26:37. It is arbitrary to understand עץ as meaning the wooden handle of the mill (Aben Ezra, and Bochart in <hi type="italic">Hieroz</hi>. i. 157, ed. Rosenmüller); the same must also be said regarding the opinion of Thenius and Nägelsbach, who refer the words to the dragging of the hand-mills, and of the wood necessary for baking bread for the comfort of the soldiers, on the march of the captives to Babylon.
entries.8dd9d9b92581f4ed18bd06407c56bb682086dd90: <reference osisRef="Lam.5.15-Lam.5.16">Lam 5:15-16</reference> <div eID="gen14750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14751" type="x-p"/> Under the pressure of such circumstances, all public meetings and amusements have ceased. "The elders cease from the fate." The gate was the place of assembly for the people, not merely for deliberating upon public affairs (Rth 4:15; <reference osisRef="Josh.20.4">Jos 20:4</reference>), but also "for social entertainment (since there were no refreshment-rooms, coffeehouses, and public baths, such as are now to be found in the East), or even for quiet enjoyment in looking at the motley multitude of passers-by; <reference osisRef="Gen.19.1">Gen 19:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.4.18">1Sa 4:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.18">1Sa 9:18</reference>; Job 29:7" (Winer’s <hi type="italic">Bibl. R.W.B. s.v. Thor</hi>). That the gate is here to be regarded as a place of entertainment and amusement, is shown by the parallel member, "young men cease from their instrumental music;" cf. Lam 1:4. On <reference osisRef="Lam.5.15">Lam 5:15</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.7.34">Jer 7:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.16.9">Jer 16:9</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Jer.31.13">Jer 31:13</reference>; Psa 30:12. Lastly, in <reference osisRef="Lam.5.16">Lam 5:16</reference>, the writer sums up the whole of the misery in the complaint, "The crown of our head is fallen! woe unto us, for we have sinned," i.e., we suffer the punishment for our sins. "The <hi type="italic">fallen crown</hi> can only be a figurative expression for the honourable position of the people in its entirety, but which is now lost." Such is the view which Ewald rightly takes; on the other hand, the interpretation of Thenius, that "the 'crown of our head' is nothing else than Zion, together with its palaces, placed on Jerusalem, as it were on the head [of the country], and adorning it," deserves mention simply as a curious specimen of exegetical fancy. Nägelsbach has gone too far in restricting the figurative expression to the crown of Jerusalem, which consists in her being mistress among the nations, a princess among the regions of the earth (<reference osisRef="Lam.1.1">Lam 1:1</reference>), the perfection of beauty, and the joy of the whole earth (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.15">Lam 2:15</reference>); for "our crown" is not equivalent to Jerusalem, or a crown on the head of Jerusalem.
entries.8cc831ebef8f9a426282be6927a415cdd6ba4238: <reference osisRef="Lam.5.17-Lam.5.18">Lam 5:17-18</reference> <div eID="gen14751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14752" type="x-p"/> The request that the judgment of wrath may be averted, and that the former gracious condition may be restored. <reference osisRef="Lam.5.17">Lam 5:17</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lam.5.18">Lam 5:18</reference> form the transition to the request in <reference osisRef="Lam.5.19">Lam 5:19</reference>-22. "Because of this" and "because of these [things]" refer mainly to what precedes, yet not in such a way as that the former must be referred to the fact that sin has been committed, and the latter to the suffering. The two halves of the verse are unmistakeably parallel; the sickening of the heart is essentially similar to the dimness coming on the eyes, the former indicating the sorrow of the soul, while the latter is the expression of this sorrow in tears. "Because of this (viz., because of the misery hitherto complained of) the heart has become sick," and the grief of the heart finds vent in tears, in consequence of which the eyes have become dim; cf. Lam 2:11. But this sorrow culminates in the view taken of the desolation of Mount Zion, which receives consideration, not because of its splendid palaces (Thenius), but as the holy mountain on which the house of God stood, for "Zion" comprehended Moriah; see on <reference osisRef="Ps.2.6">Psa 2:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.9.12">Psa 9:12</reference>; Psa 76:3. The glory formerly attaching to Mount Zion (<reference osisRef="Ps.48.3">Psa 48:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.50.2">Psa 50:2</reference>) is departed; the mountain has been so much laid waste, that jackals roam on it. שׁוּעלים are not properly foxes, but jackals (as in <reference osisRef="Ps.63.11">Psa 63:11</reference>), which lodge among the ruins. הלּך is an intensive form, meaning to rove or roam about.
entries.8aab93723b2f0487289f6f6fd17d7a1910402ba7: <reference osisRef="Lam.5.19-Lam.5.20">Lam 5:19-20</reference> <div eID="gen14752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14753" type="x-p"/> The glory of Zion, the earthly habitation of the Lord, is at an end, but the throne of the Lord endures eternally. Through this thought, the lamentation rises to the prayer that the Lord may not forsake His people for ever, but re-establish His kingdom on the earth. "Thou, O Jahveh, art enthroned eternally." This thought is expressed as the ground of hope, in nearly the same words as are found in Psa 102:13. Jahveh is the God of salvation. Since His throne endures eternally in heaven, He cannot let His kingdom perish on the earth. On this is founded the request, "Why wilt Thou forget us for ever, forsake us for a length of days (i.e., through life, always, <reference osisRef="Ps.23.6">Psa 23:6</reference>)?" This the Lord cannot do, because of His grace. From this is developed the further request (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.21">Lam 5:21</reference>), "Lead us back to Thyself, that we may return." We must not restrict השׁיב and שׁוּב to conversion to the Lord (Kalkschmidt, Ewald, Vaihinger, Gerlach); they signify the re-establishment of the gracious relation, which is, of course, impossible without repentance and conversion on the part of Israel. It is wrong to refer the words to the restoration of the people to their native land, or to the re-establishment of the theocracy (Dathe, Thenius), because it is not the exiles who address this petition to the Lord. The mode in which we are to understand the "bringing back to Jahveh" is shown in the second hemistich, "renew our days, as they were in former times," i.e., vouchsafe to us again the life (or state of grace) which we enjoyed in former times. In <reference osisRef="Lam.5.22">Lam 5:22</reference> this request is based on an argument introduced in a negative form. כּי אם, after a negative clause, signifies <hi type="italic">nisi</hi>, but (Ger. <hi type="italic">sondern</hi>). This meaning developed into that of a strong limitation (cf. Ewald, §356), unless = provided that. Thus literally here: "unless Thou hast utterly rejected us, - art very wroth against us." This case, however, is merely stated as a possibility, the actual occurrence of which is out of the question. The idea is the same as that expressed by Jeremiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.19">Jer 14:19</reference>) in the form of a question, in order to give greater emphasis to his intercession for his nation. The Lord cannot have utterly rejected His people Israel, because He would thereby make His name to be despised in the eyes of the nations (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.21">Jer 14:21</reference>). Thus terminates this lamentation, with a request for whose fulfilment faith can hope with confidence.
entries.f6c29699d7c97b89fa00363c6feb10a8bd596a4a: <reference osisRef="Lam.5.21-Lam.5.22">Lam 5:21-22</reference> <div eID="gen14753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14754" type="x-p"/> In many Hebrew MSS <reference osisRef="Lam.5.21">Lam 5:21</reference> is found repeated after <reference osisRef="Lam.5.22">Lam 5:22</reference>, to make the whole more suitable for public reading in the synagogue, that the poem may not end with the mention of the wrath of God, as is the case also at the close of Isaiah, Malachi, and Ecclesiastes: the intention is, to conclude with words of comfort. But v. 22, rightly understood, did not require this repetition: for, as Rhabanas has already remarked in <hi type="italic">Ghisleri commentar</hi>. on v. 22: <hi type="italic">non haec quasi desperando de salute populi sui locutus est, sed ut dolorem suum nimium de contritione et objectione diutina gentis suae manifestaret</hi>. This conclusion entirely agrees with the character of the Lamentations, in which complaint and supplication should continue to the end, - not, however, without an element of hope, although the latter may not rise to the heights of joyful victory, but, as Gerlach expresses himself, "merely glimmers from afar, like the morning star through the clouds, which does not indeed itself dispel the shadows of the night, though it announces that the rising of the sun is near, and that it shall obtain the victory."  <chapter eID="Lam.5"/> <div eID="gen14754" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen14522" osisID="Lam" type="book"/>

entries.3bea3048bf7846ae1be2925c0a7b0128d16ad9c7:
This prayer ought to be read as unconnected with the Lamentations, for the initial letters of the verses are not written according to the order of the Alphabet; yet it is a complaint rather than a prayer; for Jeremiah mentions those things which had happened to the people in their extreme calamity in order to turn God to compassion and mercy.
He says first, Remember what has happened to us; and then in the second part he explains himself, Look and see our reproach Now the words, though brief and concise, yet contain a useful doctrine — that God is pleased to bring help to the miserable when their evils come to an account before him, especially when they are unjustly oppressed. It is, indeed, certain that nothing is unknown to God, but this mode of speaking is according to the perceptions of men; for we think that God disregards our miseries, or we imagine that his back is turned to us when he does not immediately succor us. But as I have said, he is simply to be asked to look on our evils, for we know what he testifies of himself; so that as he claims to himself the office of helping the miserable and the unjustly oppressed, we ought to acquiesce in this consolation, that as soon as he is pleased to look on the evils we suffer, aid is at the same time prepared for us.
There is mention especially made of reproach, that the indignity might move God the more: for it was for this end that he took the people under his protection, that they might be for his glory and honor, as Moses says. As, then, it was God’s will that the riches of his glory should appear in that people, nothing could have been more inconsistent that that instead of glory they should have nothing but disgrace and reproach. This, then, is the reason why the Prophet makes a special mention of the reproach of the people. It follows, —
Lamentations 5:2
2. Our inheritance is turned to strangers, our houses to aliens.
2. Haereditas nostra devoluta est ad exteros, domus nostrae ad alienos.
entries.b7d27100d2c4ed4778e5fbf2f2a3354f26ee3061:
